cards.title: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis

depth.text: a proof of the **Riemann Hypothesis** has been checked by several **independent computer programs**

Levent Alpöge's library has **17 million lines of code** and its exported proof was checked by Lean's official kernel, **con-leche and con-ron**, plus several third-party checkers. The Lean and Mathlib communities say the statement matches Mathlib's and **certify the proof as correct**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say multiple independent checkers make a mistaken proof vanishingly unlikely; others say the checkers may not be independent enough to justify full confidence.

comments.text: If you have a physics background and want to contribute to breakthroughs like this, check Physlib (counterpart to Lean's Mathlib). It's making quick progress and is part of the Lean community. https://physlib.io

While still possible, the proof exploiting a bug is vanishingly small now. Following a few bugs and bad proofs this year, there are a number of different implementations, in different languages, and with different levels of proofs of their consistency. con-leche and con-ron are the heavy hitters, with consistency proofs of themselves. So for RH to be false, there'd have to be a bug in all the…

A fake refutation of the Collatz conjecture already got through one of these independent checkers in the past. What's harder, proving GRH or finding a way to get through every checker (which aren't as independent as they are sometimes touted to be)? In this case there was a human expert in the loop so it's much less likely the model hacked its way through the problem without the expert noticing…
If I understand correctly, for the purpose of the proof Claude formalized a huge chunk of all modern math. So it's a big result not only for GRH, but math foundations and formalization.
We need to give Levent a lot of credit for this. As much as we talk about Claude proving it, Levent seems to have a rare talent for getting the most out of it.

cards.title: My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%

depth.text: someone found their **monitor** was dropping network packets and **cutting download speeds by 75%**

Through the monitor, the old adapter’s buffer filled when it couldn’t hand data to the Mac fast enough, and packets got dropped. A second adapter sent **bigger bursts** and dropped no frames in the tests; flow control brought downloads to around **2 Gbps**, though the author didn’t want it always on because it can add latency elsewhere.

comments.text: I recently had this same problem with a multigig copper SFP+ module. These SFP+ modules (usually) advertise 10Gbps to the NIC they're plugged in, but will negotiate lower speeds on the copper side. So when NIC tries to send to SFP+ at higher rate than whatever speed SFP+ has negotiated internally, the SFP+ module will just drop a bunch of packets and incur a significant hit in throughput. These…

It turns out that Ghostty uses io_uring, and even if…

cards.title: RCE in Gnupg

A **crafted, very long user ID** in an OpenPGP key can trigger a **double free**, which can expose application data through signed data. The advisory says remote code execution can't be ruled out and recommends an update to **GPGME 2.3.1**.

cards.camps: Two camps: the advisory says remote code execution can't be ruled out; one commenter says it's a double-free bug, not an RCE chain.

comments.text: Reportedly fixed by Red Hat 5 years ago based on the output from conventional tools, but missed by upstream: https://gitlab.com/redhat/centos-stream/rpms/gpgme/-/blob/c9...

Initially we set 2026-11-25 for a coordinated disclosure;
due to the new Ruby2Shell bug GitLab had to update earlier

- Most mail clients
- Many XMPP clients

- Flatpack

cards.title: Re: Riemann

depth.text: someone says a claimed **Riemann proof** with Claude makes people feel **sidelined** by AI

The announcement claims its method extends to the **Generalized Riemann Hypothesis** and that the arguments were formalized without assumptions. The writer contrasts its praise of **Claude** with Diego Rivera’s mural, arguing people are cast as **passive recipients**; commenters split between seeing AI as a human-directed tool and fearing it makes human intelligence feel less valuable.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say AI is a human-directed tool; others fear it makes human intelligence and purpose feel less valuable.

comments.text: I could not have solved GRH with Claude, openAI, DeepSeek or any other AI. Neither could 99.99% of you. AI is a tool, like a calculator that helped mathematicians long time ago calculate sine and cosine faster than we could, then computers, then the internet, now AI. Somebody has to use the tool and input the right parameters to get the right results. AI only searched for all the knowledge that…

If the measure of man is his ability so prove theorems, then the machines clearly outstripped most of us already.
But by that measure, most of us had already been beaten by other men. I'll never be the next Euler or von Neumann or Einstein, and I'll confess to occasional pangs of regret that I'll never reach those peaks.
But mostly, I just enjoy learning about math and science, and delight in the…

> Why should we explore, discover, invent, succeed, become more, struggle, win, become divine? We don’t want to be more. We don’t want anything. why did i buy a skateboard? why did i break my arm riding it? why cant i wait to do it again? same reason we're in tar pits :) there's something more you can almost taste when you're the only one there
This post resonates a lot with me. It's depressing to see so many people rooting for a future in which human intelligence becomes irrelevant.

He’s right, it does read like a suicide note. It is precisely the tone of a terminal patient praising the skill, the care, the infinite patience of the doctor euthanizing him. That’s affected me quite heavily. I think I should probably spend the day offline, actually.

cards.title: DreamCoder: Coding harness and IDE from the author of Mastering Emacs

depth.text: someone built **DreamCoder**, a **browser-based coding harness** for juggling AI coding agents

The author says it took **fifteen months** to build, and panes can be arranged across **workspaces**; a **minimap** shows which are working or blocked. It’s designed for mouse and keyboard use, while full Emacs key bindings are still parked because browsers block some key combinations.

cards.camps: Two camps: fans praise its fresh interface and agent-management approach; critics say the market is saturated and the article offers no metrics for why it is better.

comments.text: I built https://smalldocs.org / https://github.com/espressoplease/smalldocs to handle some of the problems Mickey is trying to solve. It's a cli your agent can call to open up a markdown file in the browser with richer-than-normal formatting options. Here's an example SmallDoc that has a few formatting examples (mermaid diagrams, charts, etc.)…

I just read the whole announcement and boy I wish more text was written like this. Full of history, facts, and reasoning. Beautifully written. (I recognise it is a tad long of you just want to get cracking with it.) A very nice refresher in this age. I’ll be trying it out soon. Hopefully it does sandboxing and dealing with antigravity and codex well.

It's interesting (and probably correct) how much this focuses on the UI. I also looked (/am looking) at Lisp and AI, but I went with Clojure and zero-ed in on the REPL driven development. The high level idea is that a session maps to a namespace in Clojure. When you create a new session, it makes a new namespace, injects tools that are bound to that session into it, and then swaps you into that…

Relatedly, I have installed my customized emacs inside a container that also has codex and a bunch of other niceties. In short, having Codex and emacs side-by-side super-charges the concept of emacs. Why? Because you can ask AI to write emacs lisp quickly molding the coding environment you want for whatever task you are trying to achieve. And the container aspect makes the whole development…
Very interesting, in deed. I think it is one of the correct ways to harness all the power of AI. A set of workers doing your job in a very clear way.

cards.title: Backblaze Notice at Collection and Privacy Policy

depth.text: Backblaze says it **shared some customer information** with **ad networks** and offers an **opt-out**

The policy says it sold or shared **identifiers, internet activity, commercial information, and geolocation data** with advertising networks and analytics providers for targeted ads in the preceding 12 months. One commenter says Backblaze’s CCPA FAQ says **uploaded files** aren’t personal information and aren’t sold or shared; another calls the opt-out a **dark pattern**.

cards.camps: Two camps: critics say sharing data for ads undermines trust; others stress uploaded files aren't sold or shared, and one commenter suspects the sharing is website visits and signups.

comments.text: You can opt out of most of everything here. Sure, it appears to be a dark pattern opt out process. Sucks, been using these guys for years, hate to see them go this route. https://preferences.backblaze.com/

I know it sucks but it's worth pointing out that Backblaze explicitly distinguishes personal information from the files customers upload. Their CCPA FAQ[0] says that uploaded files are not included in the definition of personal information and that they do not sell or share those files. [0] https://help.backblaze.com/hc/en-us/articles/360040703654-Ca...

good thing all my data with this is encrypted from my end haha. Also, just gonna pimp out https://github.com/afreidah/s3-orchestrator shamelessly here...if you put it between your clients and the backend it is easy to have your data in multiple places and a cloud migration is as simple as having your clients make requests to b2 through s3-orchestrator, add your new backend you want to migrate to…

Also note: at least on MacOS, the Backblaze backup install process creates a world-readable directory that contains a world-readable file that lists ALL files to be backed up across all users. This is a security issue if you have a multi-user setup and you don't want your filenames leaked across users. Any user on the system can read this file list. Backblaze was uninterested in discussing this…

Is the data the info about your account and computer environment details? (Location, name, os, apps running on your computer, etc...) Or is it actually the data you are backing up? Are they reading your files to mine for data to sell? Or both? I think selling any of this data, account, environment, actual files, all of this is abhorrent.

cards.title: What people are building, discovered through new domains

depth.text: someone built a tracker that spots **new product companies** when their **websites go live**

The site scans around **100,000 newly observed domains** each day and tracks changes like pricing, apps, or hiring. Its listings are **produced automatically**; nothing is verified by a person, and the site says to judge each startup from the whole record.

cards.camps: Two camps: some like the idea and the thumbnails; others call the listings slop or say the pages barely explain what the products solve.

comments.text:
What Hacker News has been building since 2009?
I have compiled 23,935 answers to “What are you working on?” from 14,897 people on https://stillworkingonit.vercel.app/
I wouldn't want to be GitHub's DevOps team right now. The explosion in usage must be nigh-overwhelming.
I thought I was running out of interesting ideas, browsing this site shows there isn't anything obvious that's truly useful.
Isn't it the first principle of a product's landing page to say what it solves? Almost none of these do..
Interesting the ratio of physical hardware products versus software to me, only 94 out of 3,222 in U.S.

cards.title: GIMP now has UI tests

depth.text: GIMP now **tests its real interface** automatically, checking that **menus, dialogs and tools** still work
The **13 tests** check jobs like exporting a correct PNG and selecting a tool from the toolbox. Each runs GIMP in a **small, hidden desktop**, so it can work without a screen.

cards.camps: Two camps: some welcome the tests as a good first step; others say GIMP needs a more intuitive UI or that AI could write many more tests.

comments.text: > We have 13 tests at this time. Does GIMP have a very restrictive AI policy or something? I get not wanting to ship a gigantic pile of UI tests without thorough review, but basically any model released in the last six months would be able to write UI tests covering every single control in an afternoon.
This is really good. So much of this tech like ui tests was built for the web, and it can be a pain to get working for plain old GUI apps

> So it coult not tell us if a dialog opens, It feels good when I see spelling mistakes. It feels organic, human-sourced, non-AI. It feels like a good old village again. BTW I love GIMP for everything it did to the world of graphics work. Such an awesome thing. Thank you folks.

I created all the designs for flyers, announcements, invitations etc. in Affinity for my wife. I migrated to Linux and didn't like any of the apps. I was lost. Then Affinity announced they'll add Linux support. But for some time now my wife just uses Codex/Claude to do her day-to-day nothing special design work. I feel, just like ArtCraft, Gimp will not be relevant in some years (months?).

Funny how GIMP spawned the Gimp Toolkit, aka GTK, which is widely used in Linux, and yet GIMP's own UI seems to have long languished as a rather outdated design. Glad that they have tests, though, and hope they continue to improve it.

glossary.Riemann Hypothesis: A famous math question about the pattern behind where prime numbers appear.

glossary.theorem: A mathematical statement shown to be true through reasoning.
glossary.SWE: Software engineering: work that involves building and maintaining software.

glossary.SaaS: Software as a Service: software you access over the internet, with the provider running it for you.
glossary.PR: Pull request: a proposed code change shared so others can review it.
glossary.high-agency: Someone who takes initiative and sees a task through without waiting to be told each step.
glossary.MVP: Minimum viable product: the simplest version of a product that people can try.
glossary.GTM: Go-to-market: the work of getting a product in front of customers and selling it.

glossary.system design: Planning how the parts of a software system fit together to do a job.
glossary.lead azide: An explosive chemical whose crystals can detonate if they impact each other.
glossary.crystallize: When a liquid forms solid crystals.
glossary.plume: A cloud of smoke, dust, or other material moving through the air.
glossary.flow control: A way for a receiving device to tell the sender to pause so it can catch up.
glossary.buffer: A small holding space for audio that gives the system time to process it.
glossary.burst: A short batch of data sent together before the device waits for a reply.
glossary.latency: The time between doing something and seeing the device respond.
glossary.GPGME: A piece of software that other programs use for GnuPG features; this advisory says the bug is in it.
glossary.OpenPGP: A format used for keys and for signing or encrypting messages.
glossary.double free: A bug where a program marks the same piece of memory as free twice, which can confuse or crash it.
glossary.RCE: Remote Code Execution: a flaw that lets an attacker make a computer run their commands from somewhere else.
glossary.Lisp: A family of programming languages that writes code using nested groups of words and expressions.
glossary.macro: A tool that lets programmers add language features or transform code before it runs.
glossary.REPL: Read-Eval-Print Loop: a prompt where you enter a command and see the result right away.
glossary.persistent data structure: A way to make changes without overwriting the old data, so earlier versions remain available.
glossary.pure function: A function that returns an answer without changing anything outside itself.
glossary.concurrency: A program handling multiple tasks at once, with the tasks sometimes taking turns.
glossary.APK: The file you download to install an Android app.
glossary.WASM: WebAssembly: a way for an app to run plug-ins written in other programming languages.
glossary.JIT: Just-in-time compilation: compiling a program as it runs, rather than beforehand.
glossary.Rust: A programming language; commenters say 37signals used it for the Hey backend.
glossary.compatibility layer: Software that helps a program made for one system run on a different system.
glossary.NDK: Native Development Kit: Android's tools for making apps with code that talks directly to the device.
glossary.Dalvik: Android's system for running app code written in Java.
glossary.syscall: A request a program sends to the operating system to do something on its behalf.
glossary.sandboxing: Restricting what a program can access so it cannot freely affect the rest of the system.
glossary.DEX: Dalvik Executable: a file format that holds Android app code.
glossary.FPGA: Field-programmable gate array: a chip that can be set up for different hardware jobs after it is made.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.inference: When an AI uses what it learned to answer or act, instead of being trained.
glossary.ternary weights: Model values limited to three choices, which can make them take less space.
glossary.bit-exact: Matching exactly at the byte level, not just looking similar.
glossary.formal verification: Checking a claim using precise rules, often with a computer.
glossary.NAS: Network-attached storage: storage connected to your home network so other devices can reach its files.
glossary.FAT12: File Allocation Table 12: a way some disks organize files so a computer can find them.
glossary.root folder: The main folder on a disk, where files sit without being inside another folder.

glossary.equatorial ridge: A raised strip that runs around the middle of an object.
glossary.moonlet: A small natural body that orbits a larger one, like a little moon.

glossary.backward compatibility: Keeping older app behavior working when changes are made.

glossary.Generalized Riemann Hypothesis: A famous conjecture about where certain mathematical functions become zero, tied to how prime numbers are distributed.
glossary.stochastic parrots: A mocking label for language models that suggests they repeat learned patterns without really understanding them.
glossary.DAT: Digital Audio Tape: a tape format used to record sound digitally.

glossary.CSS framework: A collection of ready-made styles that helps developers design webpages without writing every style from scratch.

glossary.domain: A website's address on the internet.

glossary.accessibility information: Details a program provides so tools such as screen readers can understand its buttons and menus.
